 A crash in pending home sales is the latest sign that activity in the US housing market is grinding to a halt, pressured by high mortgage rates and stubbornly high prices. 
 Pending sales of existing homes in the US dropped to a record low in the month of October, marking the second straight month the data point has hit an all-time low, according to data from the National Association of Realtors.
 Pending sales dropped 4.7% from the prior record low recorded in September. Last month's figures represented a 16.7% drop in pending home sales recorded in October of last year, attesting to the severity of the housing slowdown as elevated home prices and higher rates shoo buyers away from the market.
 The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate clocked in at 7.11% the last week, according to Freddie Mac data, reflecting a sharp increase in home borrowing costs over the last year, though the rate is down from its 7.4% peak in mid-October.
 The recent sharp spike in mortgage rates suggests contract signings may be at a "low point" in this housing cycle, Lawrence Yun, the chief economist at the NAR, said. The housing market could be on pace to see the lowest number of existing home sales by year-end since the mid-90s, he added.
 "It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the US population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans," Yun said.
 The housing market has been mired in a yearslong slowdown that forecasters don't think stands to improve anytime soon, given that rates look poised to stay higher for longer.
 The scale of October's pending sales decline suggests that existing home sales will continue to drop over the fourth quarter, Capital Economics said. The firm estimated that existing home sales would average 3.7 million a year in the last three months of the year, the weakest pace since the Great Financial Crisis.
 Previously, the research firm predicted that 2026 was on track to be the weakest year for home sales in more than a decade, with mortgage rates poised to remain above 6% for at least two more years.
